extras.def: Why supply cannot respond quickly to high prices, and why copper cycles run long in both directions.

extras.label: Electric vehicle copper use
extras.def: The structural demand story: electrification needs vastly more copper per unit than what it replaces.

assets.what_it_is: The metal that conducts electricity. If the world electrifies — cars, grids, data centres, air conditioning — it runs on copper, and there is no cheap substitute.
assets.own: Mostly a signal, and only awkwardly a holding. Indian retail investors have no clean copper fund: there is no copper ETF here. What copper is genuinely useful for is reading the world — a rising copper price means global industry is busy, which tells you something true about Indian metal shares, industrial shares and the rupee.

returns.label: Inflation over time
returns.def: Industrial metals broadly track the general price level over long periods.

returns.label: Electrification demand
returns.def: Grid investment, electric vehicles and data centres genuinely need more copper than existing supply plans provide.

returns.label: Valuation drift
returns.def: Somewhat above its own real-price average, so a modest drag.

returns.label: Income
returns.def: None. Holding a metal pays nothing, and futures-based products carry a rolling cost.

assets.return_note: Roughly 5-6% a year, and not really the point. Copper's value to you is as an indicator: it usually turns before Indian industrial and metal shares do.

history.label: 2011 to 2016
history.value: Fell about 55% as Chinese construction slowed

assets.worst_fall: Fell about 65% in 2008; fell 55% over the five years to 2016
drivers_up: Electrification — grids, electric vehicles, air conditioning and data centres
Chinese stimulus aimed at construction and infrastructure
Years of under-investment in new mines, which cannot be fixed quickly
A weak dollar
drivers_down: Global recession — copper is the first commodity to signal an industrial slowdown
Chinese property weakness, still the largest single source of demand
Substitution: aluminium replaces copper in some wiring when the price gap gets extreme
New mine supply finally arriving from Africa and South America
assets.wins_when: Growth is strong and global industry is expanding; it is the earliest and most reliable casualty of a slowdown
assets.role: A dashboard instrument more than a holding. If you want the electrification theme in a portfolio, Indian metal shares or a global natural-resources fund give you it in an investable, regulated wrapper.

how_to_invest.route: There is no Indian copper ETF
how_to_invest.note: Worth stating plainly: unlike gold and silver, SEBI has not permitted a physical copper ETF. Anyone telling you they have a simple copper fund is selling you something else.

how_to_invest.examples: Hindalco, Vedanta, or a Nifty Metal index fund
how_to_invest.cost: 0.3-0.5% a year for the index fund
how_to_invest.tax: 12.5% above ₹1.25 lakh of gains after a year
how_to_invest.note: The practical route. You get copper and aluminium exposure plus company risk — these firms are leveraged to the metal price rather than equal to it.

how_to_invest.examples: International commodity and resources feeder funds
how_to_invest.tax: 12.5% after two years, as a non-equity fund
how_to_invest.note: Owns global miners including the big copper producers. Subject to the overall industry cap on overseas investment, so schemes sometimes stop taking money.

how_to_invest.examples: Commodity exchange contracts
how_to_invest.note: Leveraged and expiry-dated. Genuinely not an investment vehicle; listed here only so you know what it is when someone mentions it.

assets.tax: Depends entirely on the wrapper — equity rules for metal shares, non-equity rules for global funds, business income for futures.
watch: The copper price itself, as a global growth signal — it often turns before equity markets do
Chinese property starts and grid investment announcements
Copper inventories on the London and Shanghai exchanges
assets.verdict: Read it, do not necessarily own it. Copper is the most informative price in the commodity world — it tells you whether global industry is genuinely busy, and it usually turns before Indian metal and industrial shares do, which makes it free intelligence. The demand story is also the most credible of any commodity: electrifying transport and rebuilding grids needs far more copper than the mines being planned will supply, and new mines take ten to fifteen years. But there is no honest retail route to own it in India, and the routes that exist — miners, futures — give you something other than copper. Use it as a dashboard, and take the theme through metal shares if you want it in your portfolio.

families.label: Property
families.note: The asset most Indian families already own too much of. Rent is the earnings; everything else is hope about the price.

assets.name: Property you buy directly
assets.proxy: Residential prices in the top 8 cities
assets.metric_def: The annual rent divided by what the property cost. A 2.8% yield means a ₹1 crore flat brings in ₹2.8 lakh of rent a year — before repairs, property tax, broker fees and the months it sits empty. Here a LOW number means expensive.

extras.label: Price to annual income
extras.def: A typical city flat costs roughly eleven years of a typical buyer's household income. Around 5x is considered affordable internationally.

extras.label: Net yield after costs
extras.def: What actually reaches you after maintenance, property tax, and an empty month or two a year. Compare this with 6.6% from a government bond.

extras.label: Cost to buy and sell
extras.def: Stamp duty, registration, brokerage and legal work. You start well behind, which is why property needs years to work.

assets.what_it_is: A flat, a house or a plot, bought with your own money and usually a large loan. The asset most Indian families already hold most of their wealth in.
assets.own: A single, illiquid, undiversified, leveraged asset in one specific location — plus a small business you now run, involving tenants, repairs and paperwork. That is not an argument against it; it is a description that most buyers skip. Its two real advantages are also rarely stated: cheap long-term leverage that no other asset offers a retail investor, and the fact that you cannot panic-sell it at 10am on a bad day.

returns.label: Rent, after costs
returns.def: What actually reaches you after maintenance, tax and vacancy. Far less than the headline yield.

returns.label: Price growth
returns.def: Long-run Indian city price growth, roughly inflation plus a little. Individual cities and micro-markets vary enormously.

returns.label: Valuation drift
returns.def: Rental yields are near a fifteen-year low, which means prices have already run ahead of rents. Some of that gap tends to close.

assets.return_note: About 6-7% a year unleveraged — less than a government bond plus a little. A home loan changes this arithmetic substantially in both directions: it multiplies the gain and the loss, and the loan is the real reason property has built wealth in India.

history.label: Last 10 years
history.value: About 5-6% a year in the big cities

history.label: 2013 to 2020
history.value: Roughly flat in real terms for seven years across most Indian cities

assets.worst_fall: Prices rarely fall on paper in India — they stop moving, and inflation does the damage quietly. Mumbai and Delhi lost 20-30% of real value between 2013 and 2020 with headline prices barely changing
drivers_up: Home loan rates falling, which is what actually decides affordability
Genuine income growth and urbanisation
Developer consolidation after 2018, leaving fewer and better builders
The post-2020 preference for larger homes, which is real and lasting
drivers_down: Affordability: eleven times income is stretched by any historical standard
Rental yields near record lows, meaning the price is not supported by the income
Rising interest rates, which hit this asset harder than any other
Enormous hidden costs — stamp duty, brokerage, maintenance — that never appear in the return people quote
assets.wins_when: Rates are falling and incomes are rising; it is the hardest asset to exit when you need money
assets.role: One home to live in is a life decision, not a portfolio decision, and it is usually a good one — the forced saving and the cheap leverage do real work. A second property as an investment deserves the same scrutiny as any other asset, and on the numbers it currently compares poorly with simply lending the money out.

how_to_invest.route: Buy a home to live in
how_to_invest.examples: Your own house or flat
how_to_invest.tax: Home loan interest deduction up to ₹2 lakh a year; no capital gains tax if you reinvest in another house
how_to_invest.note: The strongest case for property. You save forced monthly amounts, you cannot sell in a panic, and you remove rent from your expenses forever.

how_to_invest.route: A second property, to let out
how_to_invest.examples: An investment flat
how_to_invest.cost: Same transaction costs, plus your time
how_to_invest.tax: Rent taxed at your slab after a 30% standard deduction; 12.5% on gains after two years
how_to_invest.note: This is where the arithmetic gets hard. Net yield near 1.8% against 6.6% from a bond, plus tenant risk, repairs and no liquidity. Do this for a specific reason, not by default.

how_to_invest.examples: Listed real estate investment trusts
how_to_invest.note: Property income without the paperwork or the ₹1 crore ticket. Currently pays more than double the net rental yield on a flat.

how_to_invest.examples: Platforms offering slices of commercial buildings, now regulated as small REITs
how_to_invest.note: Newly brought under SEBI rules, which is an improvement. Still illiquid, still concentrated in one building, and the fees deserve close reading.

assets.tax: Rent is added to your income and taxed at your slab, after a 30% standard deduction. Gains after two years are taxed at 12.5% without indexation, or 20% with indexation for properties bought before July 2024 — you may choose whichever is lower.
watch: Home loan rates, the single biggest driver of Indian property prices
Rental yields in your own city — if they fall below 2.5%, prices are running on hope
Unsold inventory months, published quarterly by property consultancies
assets.verdict: A fine place to live and a mediocre investment at today's prices. The numbers are uncomfortable and worth saying plainly: a city flat yields about 2.8% in rent, roughly 1.8% after real costs, while lending the same money to the Government of India pays 6.6% with no tenant and no repairs. That gap means years of future rent increases are already in the price. Property's genuine advantages are leverage — no other asset lets an ordinary person borrow at 8.5% for twenty years — and the fact that you cannot sell it in a panic, which has quietly made more Indian families wealthy than any clever strategy. Buy one to live in with those advantages in mind. For a second one, compare it honestly with a REIT and a bond before signing.

assets.name: Rent from offices & malls (REITs)
assets.metric_def: The cash paid out to unit holders each year, as a percentage of the unit price. A 6.4% yield means ₹6,400 a year on a ₹1 lakh holding. A HIGH number means cheap — you are getting more income for your money.

extras.label: Yield versus the 10-year bond
extras.def: REITs currently pay about the same as a risk-free government bond, plus the possibility that rents grow. That is a reasonable starting point, not a bargain.

extras.label: Occupancy
extras.def: How much of the space is actually let. Office REITs dipped after 2020 and have largely recovered as return-to-office took hold in India.

extras.label: Legal payout requirement
extras.def: By SEBI rules a REIT must distribute at least 90% of its net cash to unit holders. That is why the income is reliable and the unit price grows slowly.

assets.what_it_is: A listed trust that owns large office parks and shopping malls, collects rent from corporate tenants, and is legally required to pass almost all of it on to you.
assets.own: A landlord's share of India's best commercial property, in units you can buy for a few hundred rupees and sell the same day. The tenants are companies on multi-year leases with built-in rent escalations, which makes the income far steadier than residential rent — and it comes without tenants calling you about a leaking tap.

composition.name: Office parks
composition.note: Embassy, Mindspace, Brookfield. Leased to global companies, usually with 5% annual rent increases written in

composition.name: Shopping malls
composition.note: Nexus Select. Rent partly linked to tenant sales, so it rises with consumer spending

returns.label: Rent paid to you
returns.def: Cash arriving in your account every quarter. The bulk of the return, and the reason to own this.

returns.label: Rent growth
returns.def: Indian commercial leases typically build in about 5% annual escalations, partly offset by re-leasing at market rates.

returns.label: Valuation drift
returns.def: Priced close to its own short history, so little help or harm from re-rating.

assets.return_note: About 10% a year, with two-thirds of it arriving as cash rather than as a price you hope someone pays later. That mix is unusual in India and genuinely useful.

history.label: Price alone
history.value: Roughly flat — nearly all the return has been the income
Fell about 25% as offices emptied, then recovered as employees returned

assets.worst_fall: Fell about 25-30% in 2020-22 when it was unclear whether offices had a future
drivers_up: Falling interest rates — a 6.4% income becomes far more attractive when bonds pay 5%
Global companies expanding their India offices, the main source of new demand
Contractual rent escalations, which arrive whatever the market does
Malls doing well as consumer spending rises
drivers_down: Rising interest rates: when a safe bond pays 8%, a 6.4% property income looks poor
Permanent remote or hybrid working reducing how much office space companies need
New supply in Bengaluru and Hyderabad, where a lot is being built
Thin trading volumes, so large orders can move the price
assets.wins_when: Rates are falling and growth is steady; hurt whenever bond yields rise sharply
assets.role: The income slot in a portfolio, and the sane way to own Indian property. Five to ten per cent gives you a real quarterly cash flow that does not depend on selling anything.

how_to_invest.route: Buy REIT units on the exchange
how_to_invest.examples: Embassy Office Parks, Mindspace, Brookfield India, Nexus Select Trust
how_to_invest.tax: Split: the interest portion at your slab, the dividend portion often tax-free, and 12.5% on gains after a year
how_to_invest.note: The direct route. Each REIT is a different set of buildings in different cities — read what you are actually buying rather than treating them as interchangeable.

how_to_invest.examples: Funds tracking a basket of listed REITs and InvITs
how_to_invest.tax: Non-equity fund rules: 12.5% after two years
how_to_invest.note: Spreads the risk across all the listed trusts. A newer, simpler option if choosing between four REITs feels like guesswork.

how_to_invest.examples: Newly regulated fractional-ownership platforms
how_to_invest.note: Brought under SEBI rules in 2024, which is a genuine improvement over the unregulated version. Still illiquid and concentrated in a single building.

how_to_invest.examples: Target maturity and corporate bond funds
how_to_invest.note: Worth comparing directly. If a debt fund pays 7.4% with no property risk, a REIT needs its rent growth to justify the extra risk — which it plausibly does, but check rather than assume.

assets.tax: REIT distributions arrive in parts and are taxed differently: the interest component at your slab rate, the dividend component usually tax-free (if the REIT has not opted for a lower corporate tax rate), and any return of capital is tax-free but reduces your cost. Gains on units held over a year are taxed at 12.5%.
watch: The 10-year government bond yield — REIT prices move opposite to it
Occupancy and net absorption figures in the quarterly updates
Whether distributions per unit are actually growing, or merely being maintained
assets.verdict: The most sensible way for an Indian investor to own property, and it is priced fairly. You collect about 6.4% in cash each year from offices let to serious companies on escalating leases — roughly three and a half times the net rent on a city flat — with no stamp duty, no tenant calls, a ₹300 entry ticket and same-day liquidity. The honest limitations: it pays about the same as a risk-free government bond today, so you are being paid mainly for rent growth rather than for the risk; trading volumes are thin; and the long-term question about how much office space companies need is genuinely unsettled. Own it for the quarterly cash, judge it against the 10-year bond yield, and note that on the current numbers it beats buying a second flat comfortably.

assets.name: Roads & power lines (InvITs)
assets.metric_def: Annual cash paid out as a percentage of the unit price. A HIGH number means cheap. At 9.5% these pay well above REITs and bonds — partly as reward, partly because some of that cash is your own capital coming back.

extras.label: Yield over the 10-year bond
extras.def: A genuinely wide gap. Part of it is real compensation for risk; part reflects that a toll road has a finite life.

extras.label: Typical asset life
extras.def: The crucial difference from a REIT. A toll concession expires and the asset goes back to the government — so some of that 9.5% is capital being returned, not pure income.

extras.label: Revenue certainty
extras.value: High for grids, variable for roads
extras.def: Power transmission earns a regulated fee whatever happens. Toll roads depend on how many trucks actually pass.

assets.what_it_is: A listed trust that owns operating infrastructure — electricity transmission lines, toll roads, gas pipelines — and passes the cash it collects to unit holders.
assets.own: The tollbooth, not the construction company. These assets are already built and earning; there is no project risk. A power transmission trust is close to a regulated utility: it earns a fixed fee for keeping the lines available, almost regardless of economic conditions. Toll roads are less certain — traffic can disappoint — but even then the revenue is inflation-linked, since toll rates rise with the wholesale price index.

composition.name: Power transmission
composition.note: IndiGrid, PowerGrid InvIT. Regulated availability-based income — the most predictable cash flow in Indian markets

composition.name: Toll roads
composition.note: IRB and similar. Traffic-dependent, inflation-linked toll rates, finite concession periods

composition.name: Pipelines & other
composition.note: Gas transmission and newer categories

returns.label: Cash paid to you
returns.def: Quarterly distributions. The whole point of this asset — the return arrives now, not later.

returns.label: Growth in distributions
returns.def: Modest. Toll rates rise with inflation and trusts buy new assets, but the base assets do age.

returns.label: Capital returned, not earned
returns.def: The honest deduction. Part of that 9.5% is your own money coming back as the concession runs down, so it should not be counted as pure yield.

assets.return_note: About 9% a year, nearly all of it as cash. The critical discipline is not to spend the whole distribution — some of it is capital being returned and needs reinvesting if you want to maintain your income.

history.label: Price alone
history.value: Broadly flat to slightly down — this is an income asset, not a growth one

assets.worst_fall: Fell about 20% in March 2020; individual road trusts have fallen 30% on traffic disappointments
drivers_up: Falling interest rates, which make a 9.5% income far more valuable
The trust buying new operating assets, which extends its life and its distributions
India's grid investment programme creating a steady supply of assets to acquire
Inflation, since toll rates are contractually linked to it
drivers_down: Rising interest rates — these trade like long-duration bonds and fall when yields rise
Traffic disappointing on toll roads
Concessions expiring without replacement assets being bought
Very thin trading volumes — some of these are genuinely hard to sell in size
assets.wins_when: Rates are falling and inflation is moderate; toll-linked trusts also hold up when inflation runs hot
assets.role: A high-income diversifier for someone who needs cash flow now — retirees especially. Not a growth holding, and not a place for money you might need suddenly.

how_to_invest.route: Buy InvIT units on the exchange
how_to_invest.examples: IndiGrid, IRB InvIT, PowerGrid InvIT
how_to_invest.tax: Interest portion at your slab, dividend portion often tax-free, 12.5% on gains after a year
how_to_invest.note: The grid trusts are the more predictable of the two kinds. Check the remaining concession life before buying — a shorter life means more of the yield is capital return.

how_to_invest.examples: Funds tracking listed REITs and InvITs together
how_to_invest.note: One holding covering the whole category. Sensible if you want the income without researching each trust.

how_to_invest.examples: Institutional infrastructure trusts
how_to_invest.note: Not accessible to ordinary retail investors. Mentioned so you know why the listed universe is small — most InvIT money in India is institutional.

assets.tax: Distributions are split: interest at your slab, dividends usually tax-free, and return of capital tax-free but reducing your cost base. Gains after a year are taxed at 12.5%. The mixed treatment makes the after-tax yield genuinely different for a 30% taxpayer than the headline 9.5% suggests.
watch: The 10-year government bond yield — these are the most interest-rate-sensitive income assets in India
Remaining concession life and any new asset acquisitions
Traffic growth on the road trusts, published monthly
assets.verdict: The highest honest income available to an Indian retail investor, with one detail most people miss. A 9.5% distribution from a power transmission trust is genuinely attractive when a government bond pays 6.6%, and the grid trusts earn a regulated fee that barely notices the economy. But a toll road or a transmission concession has a finite life, so part of that 9.5% is your own capital being handed back — spend all of it and your income quietly shrinks each year. Read the remaining concession life, prefer the grid trusts for predictability, reinvest the capital-return portion, and accept that trading volumes are thin. Used properly it is one of the most useful and least understood instruments on this page.

families.label: Lending your money out
families.note: You become the lender instead of the owner. Boring by design — this is the part of a portfolio that still works when shares do not.

assets.name: Government bonds
assets.metric_def: The bond pays 6.6% a year; inflation is running near 4.5%. The difference — about 2.1% — is what you actually gain in buying power. A HIGH number means you are being paid well, so here big is good.

extras.label: Headline yield
extras.def: What a 10-year Government of India bond pays today, guaranteed, if you hold it to maturity.

extras.label: Credit risk
extras.def: The government prints the rupee, so it cannot run out of them. You can lose to inflation; you cannot lose to default.

extras.label: Price sensitivity
extras.def: Duration. If yields fall 1%, a 10-year bond gains roughly 7% in price — and loses the same if they rise.

assets.what_it_is: A loan to the Government of India. It promises you a fixed interest payment twice a year and your money back at the end. The safest rupee asset there is.
assets.own: Certainty, and a bet on interest rates. Two separate things happen here. Held to maturity, you simply collect 6.6% a year — done. Sold earlier, the price depends on what rates have done since: when rates fall, existing bonds paying 6.6% become more valuable, and their price rises. That is why bonds are the one asset that reliably goes UP when shares crash and the RBI cuts.

returns.label: Interest you lock in
returns.def: Contractual. If you hold to maturity this is your return, whatever happens in between.

returns.label: Price gain if rates fall
returns.def: An estimate of the extra return if the RBI cuts rates over the coming years, as most expect once inflation is settled.

assets.return_note: About 7% a year with genuine certainty, and more if rates fall. Compare that with the 6-7% expected from a city flat after all its costs and risks, and the case for boring becomes obvious.

history.label: 2013 to 2016
history.value: Roughly 12% a year as yields fell from 9% to 6.5%

history.label: Worst stretch, 2021-22
history.value: Lost about 3% as inflation and rate rises pushed yields up

assets.worst_fall: Government bond funds fell about 5-8% in 2013 and again in 2022 when yields rose sharply. No default risk, but real price falls when rates rise
drivers_up: The RBI cutting interest rates, which lifts the price of every existing bond
Inflation falling, which raises the real return you keep
India's inclusion in global bond indices, which brings steady foreign buying
A flight to safety in any crisis
drivers_down: Inflation surprising upward, the one thing that genuinely hurts a bondholder
The government borrowing more than expected, which means more supply of bonds
Rate rises, which push existing bond prices down
A falling rupee, which erodes what your rupees are worth globally
assets.wins_when: Rates are falling and when the world gets frightened — the mirror image of equity
assets.role: The stabiliser. This is what lets you hold shares through a crash: when equity falls 40%, bonds typically rise, and rebalancing forces you to sell the thing that went up to buy the thing that collapsed. That mechanical discipline is worth more than any forecast.

how_to_invest.route: Buy G-secs directly on RBI Retail Direct
how_to_invest.examples: RBI's own platform, free to open
how_to_invest.tax: Interest at your slab; 12.5% on gains if sold after a year
how_to_invest.note: The purest route — you lend directly to the government with no intermediary and no expense ratio. Held to maturity, the return is exactly what you signed up for.

how_to_invest.examples: Gilt funds and 10-year constant-maturity gilt funds
how_to_invest.tax: At your income slab, whenever you sell
how_to_invest.note: Easier and SIP-able, but the fund never matures — so you are permanently exposed to price swings rather than being able to wait it out.

how_to_invest.examples: Bharat Bond ETF and target-maturity index funds
how_to_invest.note: The best of both: it holds bonds to a fixed maturity date, so if you match that date to your goal you get a near-predictable return with fund convenience. Among the most underused instruments in India.

how_to_invest.examples: Any bank
how_to_invest.tax: At your slab, deducted each year even if you have not withdrawn
how_to_invest.note: Similar rate, less flexible, and taxed annually rather than on sale. A government bond is genuinely safer than a bank deposit above the ₹5 lakh insured limit.

assets.tax: Interest is added to your income and taxed at your slab — which for a 30% taxpayer turns 6.6% into about 4.6%. All debt mutual funds bought after April 2023 are taxed at slab rate regardless of holding period. Directly held bonds sold after a year qualify for 12.5% on the capital gain, which is why holding them directly can be more efficient.
watch: CPI inflation prints — the single number that decides whether your real yield holds
RBI policy statements and the tone on future rate moves
The government's borrowing calendar and fiscal deficit target
assets.verdict: The most under-owned sensible asset in India, and currently priced well. You are being paid about 2.1% above inflation to take no default risk at all, against a twenty-year average nearer 1.2% — so on this measure bonds are the cheapest thing on this page. For a 30% taxpayer, tax eats much of it, which is exactly why the direct route through RBI Retail Direct or a target maturity fund matters. The real argument for owning these is not the return, though: it is that bonds go up when shares collapse, which is what makes it psychologically possible to keep holding equity through the worst year of your investing life. Most Indian portfolios have almost none of this and are far more fragile than their owners realise.

assets.name: Company bonds & debt funds
assets.metric_def: How much more a top-rated company pays you than the government does, for lending it money. The gap is the compensation for the small chance the company cannot pay. A HIGH number means you are being paid well for that risk.

extras.label: Typical yield
extras.def: What a AAA-rated corporate bond fund currently yields, before tax.

extras.label: Default record, AAA
extras.def: Genuine AAA defaults in India are rare. The accidents have almost always been in lower-rated paper that was sold as safe.

extras.label: What went wrong before
extras.def: Every Indian debt fund disaster came from reaching for extra yield in weaker credits, not from AAA bonds.

assets.what_it_is: Lending to companies instead of the government — Reliance, HDFC, power utilities, NBFCs — usually through a mutual fund holding many such loans.
assets.own: Slightly more return for slightly more risk, and the risk is not in the average — it is in the tail. A portfolio of AAA bonds behaves almost like government bonds until one borrower fails, at which point the fund can be frozen. The lesson from IL&FS, DHFL and Franklin Templeton is identical each time: the extra yield came from lower-rated paper, and it was never enough to compensate.

returns.label: Interest you lock in
returns.def: The yield on a good-quality corporate bond portfolio today.

returns.label: Credit losses over time
returns.def: A realistic long-run allowance for the occasional borrower that cannot pay, even in a AAA portfolio.

returns.label: Price gain if rates fall
returns.def: Corporate bond funds are typically shorter-dated than gilt funds, so they gain less when rates fall — and lose less when rates rise.

assets.return_note: About 7.5% a year before tax, and roughly 5.2% after tax at the 30% slab. Steady and unexciting, which is precisely the point.

history.label: Best recent stretch
history.value: About 10% a year in 2019-20 as rates collapsed

history.label: Credit-risk funds, 2020
history.value: Some fell 15-50% or froze entirely — the cautionary tale

assets.worst_fall: High-quality corporate bond funds have rarely fallen more than 3%. Credit-risk funds chasing yield have lost half their value and gated withdrawals
drivers_up: Falling interest rates
Credit spreads narrowing as the economy strengthens
Strong company balance sheets, which is currently the case across Indian industry
drivers_down: Any default in the portfolio, which matters far more than the average yield
Rising rates, though less than for long government bonds
Liquidity drying up in a crisis — corporate bonds are hard to sell precisely when you need to
assets.wins_when: Growth is strong and boring; it is the worst place to be in a credit crisis
assets.role: The three-to-five-year money slot: a house deposit, a car, school fees. Better than a savings account, far more predictable than equity, and it should never be where you reach for extra return.

how_to_invest.examples: Corporate bond schemes, which must hold at least 80% in the top-rated paper
how_to_invest.note: The standard sensible choice. Check the portfolio yourself for anything rated below AA — if the yield looks unusually high, that is where it is coming from.

how_to_invest.examples: Bharat Bond ETF and similar, with a fixed maturity year
how_to_invest.note: Holds only government-backed or top-rated paper to a stated date. If you match the maturity to when you need the money, the outcome is close to predictable.

how_to_invest.examples: Schemes restricted to bank and public-sector paper
how_to_invest.note: By mandate the safest corporate category — it can only lend to banks and state-owned entities.

how_to_invest.examples: Bought on the exchange or via online bond platforms
how_to_invest.entry: ₹10,000, down from ₹10 lakh after SEBI reduced the minimum
how_to_invest.tax: Interest at slab; 12.5% on gains if sold after a year
how_to_invest.note: Now genuinely accessible to retail investors. Just remember a single bond is a single borrower — diversification is the whole reason funds exist.

how_to_invest.examples: Schemes that deliberately buy lower-rated paper
how_to_invest.note: The category that produced India's debt fund disasters. An extra 2% of yield does not compensate for a 30% loss, and the risk shows up all at once.

assets.tax: All debt mutual funds are taxed at your income slab regardless of how long you hold them — the indexation benefit ended in April 2023. For a 30% taxpayer a 7.4% yield becomes about 5.2%. Directly held bonds sold after a year still get 12.5% on the capital gain, which is worth knowing.
watch: The credit spread over government bonds — below 0.6 points means you are barely paid for the risk
The actual holdings of your fund, with attention to anything below AA
Any rating downgrade among large NBFCs, historically the early warning
assets.verdict: Do this boringly or do not do it at all. Lending to top-rated Indian companies pays about 7.4% against the government's 6.6% — a 0.8 point premium, slightly below the historical 1.0, so you are being paid a little less than usual for the risk. That is fine if you stay in high-quality paper, where this is a genuinely useful home for three-to-five-year money. It becomes dangerous the moment you reach for more yield: every Indian debt fund catastrophe, from IL&FS to Franklin, came from exactly that reach, and the losses arrived all at once with withdrawals frozen. Use a target maturity fund matched to when you need the money, read the holdings, and accept the unexciting number.

assets.name: Cash, FDs & liquid funds
assets.metric_label: Real return after tax and inflation
assets.metric_def: A 7% deposit, minus 30% tax, leaves 4.9%. Minus inflation of about 4.5%, you keep roughly 0.4% of real buying power. A HIGH number is good — but this number is almost never high.

extras.label: Deposit insurance limit
extras.def: What is guaranteed if a bank fails, covering principal and interest together. Above this, you are an unsecured lender to the bank.

extras.label: Liquid fund yield
extras.def: Slightly less than an FD, but taxed only when you sell rather than every year — which usually makes it better after tax.

extras.label: Access
extras.def: Liquid funds settle in one working day; some offer instant redemption up to ₹50,000.

assets.what_it_is: Money kept safe and reachable: a savings account, a bank fixed deposit, or a liquid or money-market mutual fund.
assets.own: Optionality. Cash's real value is not its return — it is the ability to act. In March 2020 the people who bought were the ones with cash, not the ones with conviction. The cost of that ability is that cash barely keeps pace with inflation, and at the 30% slab it essentially treads water forever.

returns.label: Interest earned
returns.def: A one-year fixed deposit or liquid fund yield today. Like every estimate on this page, this is a nominal rupee return before tax.

assets.return_note: 6.6% before tax — and this is the asset where what happens next matters most. Deposit interest is taxed EVERY year whether you withdraw it or not, so at the 30% slab you keep about 4.9%. Take away inflation of roughly 4.5% and you are left with about 0.4% of extra buying power a year: ₹1 lakh kept in a deposit for thirty years buys roughly what ₹1.1 lakh buys today. Perfectly correct for short-term money and quietly destructive for long-term money.

history.label: 2010 to 2013
history.value: Negative in real terms as inflation ran near 10%

assets.worst_fall: Never falls in rupee terms. That is precisely its appeal and precisely its trap — the loss is in what those rupees can buy
drivers_up: The RBI raising rates, which lifts deposit rates quickly
Falling inflation, which raises what you actually keep
Competition among banks for deposits, which is currently real
drivers_down: Inflation rising, the standing enemy of anyone holding cash
Rate cuts, which reduce what new deposits pay
Tax, deducted annually and unavoidable at the higher slabs
assets.wins_when: The world gets frightened — the only regime where holding cash actively makes you money, because it lets you buy what others must sell
assets.role: Six to twelve months of expenses as an emergency fund, plus anything you need within three years, plus a little dry powder. Every rupee beyond that is a decision to earn almost nothing for a long time.

how_to_invest.examples: Liquid and money market schemes from any fund house
how_to_invest.tax: At your slab, but only when you sell
how_to_invest.note: Usually better than an FD for a taxpayer: similar yield, no annual tax deduction, and you can withdraw any amount any day without breaking anything.

how_to_invest.examples: Any bank; small finance banks pay 1-2% more
how_to_invest.tax: At your slab, deducted every year
how_to_invest.note: Simple and insured to ₹5 lakh per bank. Spread across banks if you hold more than that. Small finance banks pay more because they are riskier — the insurance limit is the relevant number.

how_to_invest.examples: Arbitrage schemes
how_to_invest.tax: Treated as equity: 12.5% after a year, 20% within
how_to_invest.note: A quiet trick worth knowing. Arbitrage funds earn an FD-like return with FD-like stability but are taxed as equity — often the most tax-efficient way to park money for a year or more at the 30% slab.

how_to_invest.examples: Auto-sweep facilities at most banks
how_to_invest.note: Moves surplus balance into a deposit automatically and back when you spend. The least-effort improvement on a plain savings account.

assets.tax: Deposit interest is taxed at your slab each year as it accrues, whether withdrawn or not. Liquid fund gains are taxed at slab but only on sale, which defers the bill. Arbitrage funds are taxed as equity — 12.5% after a year — which makes them the most efficient option for a higher-rate taxpayer parking money for over a year.
watch: Your own emergency fund: months of expenses covered, reviewed once a year
The RBI's repo rate, which leads deposit rates
How much cash you are holding out of caution rather than plan — the most common expensive mistake
assets.verdict: Exactly right for three years of money and quietly ruinous for thirty. At the 30% slab a 7% deposit leaves you about 0.4% a year after tax and inflation — so ₹1 lakh parked for three decades buys roughly ₹1.1 lakh of goods. That is not safety; it is a slow, certain loss dressed as prudence. Hold six to twelve months of expenses plus anything you need within three years, and know two specific improvements: a liquid fund defers the tax an FD deducts annually, and an arbitrage fund earns an FD-like return taxed at equity rates. Cash's real job is to be the money you buy with when everyone else is selling.

assets.name: Government small savings
assets.proxy: PPF · Sukanya Samriddhi · NSC · Senior Citizen scheme
assets.metric_def: PPF pays 7.1% completely tax-free. For a 30% taxpayer that equals about 10.1% from a taxable investment — against 6.6% from a government bond. A HIGH number means a better deal, and this is the best risk-free deal available in India.
assets.metric_avg_label: Typical equivalent over the past decade

extras.label: PPF rate
extras.def: No tax on the contribution, the interest, or the maturity amount. India has almost nothing else structured this way.

extras.label: Annual limit
extras.def: The constraint. This is why PPF is a foundation rather than a whole plan.

extras.label: Sukanya Samriddhi rate
extras.def: For a daughter under ten. The single highest guaranteed tax-free rate available to any Indian citizen.

assets.what_it_is: Government-run savings schemes: Public Provident Fund, Sukanya Samriddhi for daughters, National Savings Certificates, and the Senior Citizen Savings Scheme.
assets.own: A sovereign guarantee with a tax exemption attached. The return itself is modest, but nothing is deducted — not on the way in, not on the interest, not at maturity. For someone in the 30% bracket, PPF's 7.1% is the equivalent of finding a completely safe 10.1% elsewhere, which does not exist. The cost is a fifteen-year lock-in and a ₹1.5 lakh annual cap.

returns.label: Interest earned
returns.def: The current PPF rate, reset by the government each quarter. Shown on the same basis as every other asset here — a nominal rupee return.

assets.return_note: 7.1% looks unremarkable next to equity, and the comparison misses the entire point: nothing is taxed, at any stage. For a 30% taxpayer that makes it equivalent to about 10.1% from a taxable investment — and there is no safe 10% anywhere in India. Against inflation of roughly 4.5% you keep about 2.6% of real buying power a year, six times what a fixed deposit leaves you. Judge this one on its tax-free equivalent, not on the headline number.

history.label: PPF rate today
history.value: 7.1% — the rate is reset quarterly and has drifted down with interest rates generally

assets.worst_fall: Cannot fall. The only risk is that the government reduces the rate on future interest, which it has done gradually
drivers_up: The government keeping rates above market levels for political reasons, which it has done consistently
Your own tax bracket — the higher it is, the more the exemption is worth
Compounding across fifteen years with nothing deducted along the way
drivers_down: Quarterly rate resets, which have trended downward with the general level of rates
The ₹1.5 lakh annual cap, which limits how much good this can do
A fifteen-year lock-in, with only limited partial withdrawals from year seven
Inflation, which still erodes a 7.1% return
assets.wins_when: Every regime. It is the one asset here that cannot fall in rupee terms and cannot be taxed
assets.role: The foundation, filled first. Before any debt fund or fixed deposit, a higher-rate taxpayer should use the PPF limit — and Sukanya Samriddhi if there is a daughter under ten, because 8.2% tax-free guaranteed is simply the best fixed-income deal in the country.

how_to_invest.examples: Any bank or post office; most banks allow it online
how_to_invest.tax: Fully exempt — contribution, interest and maturity
how_to_invest.note: Fifteen-year term, extendable in five-year blocks. Partial withdrawal allowed from year seven. Deposit before the 5th of the month to earn that month's interest.

how_to_invest.examples: Any bank or post office, for a daughter under ten
how_to_invest.note: 8.2% tax-free and government-guaranteed — the highest safe rate available to anyone in India. If you have an eligible daughter, this outranks every other fixed-income option here.

how_to_invest.examples: Post office
how_to_invest.tax: Interest taxable, but reinvested interest qualifies for the 80C deduction
how_to_invest.note: Five-year term. Useful when you want a shorter lock-in than PPF, though the interest is taxed.

how_to_invest.examples: Banks and post offices, age 60 and above
how_to_invest.tax: Interest taxable; ₹50,000 deduction available for seniors
how_to_invest.note: 8.2%, paid quarterly, government-guaranteed. For a retiree needing income this is difficult to beat on a risk-adjusted basis.

how_to_invest.examples: Through your employer; voluntary contributions possible
how_to_invest.tax: Exempt, unless your own contributions exceed ₹2.5 lakh a year
how_to_invest.note: 8.25% and effectively the same structure. Voluntary Provident Fund lets you add more at the same rate, up to that ₹2.5 lakh limit before interest becomes taxable.

assets.tax: PPF, Sukanya Samriddhi and EPF are exempt at all three stages — going in, while growing, and at maturity. NSC and the Senior Citizen scheme have taxable interest. Note that this is only available under the old tax regime's 80C deduction; under the new regime the deduction is gone but the tax-free interest and maturity remain.
watch: The quarterly small savings rate announcement, at the end of each quarter
Whether you have actually used the full ₹1.5 lakh PPF limit this year
Your tax regime choice, which decides whether the 80C deduction still applies to you
assets.verdict: The best risk-free deal in India, and the most widely under-used. PPF's 7.1% tax-free is equivalent to about 10.1% from a taxable investment for a 30% taxpayer — and there is no safe 10% anywhere else, because the government is deliberately paying above market to encourage household saving. Sukanya Samriddhi at 8.2% tax-free is better still if you have a daughter under ten. The genuine costs are real: a fifteen-year lock-in and a ₹1.5 lakh annual ceiling, so this cannot be a whole plan. But it should be the first fixed-income rupee you commit each year, ahead of any deposit or debt fund, and most people fill it last or not at all.

families.label: Owning the world from India
families.note: The rupee weakens over decades. Owning assets that earn in dollars is how you stop that from quietly shrinking you.

assets.name: International shares
assets.metric_def: Cyclically-adjusted PE: price divided by average inflation-adjusted profits over ten years, so one boom or bust year cannot distort it. At about 30 against a long-run average near 22, world shares — dominated by America — are priced well above normal.

extras.label: US share of world index
extras.def: A 'global' fund is mostly an American fund. That is the market's judgment, and it is also a concentration you should be aware of.

extras.label: Rupee tailwind
extras.def: The rupee has weakened roughly 3% a year against the dollar for three decades, which adds to your rupee returns automatically.

extras.label: Overseas investment limit
extras.def: The RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme cap. Generous enough that it constrains almost nobody.

assets.what_it_is: Owning Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Nestlé and Toyota from India — through an Indian mutual fund, or directly under the RBI's overseas remittance scheme.
assets.own: Dollar earnings, and the end of a single-currency bet. This is the one holding on this page that addresses a risk most Indian portfolios ignore entirely: everything you own, earn and spend is in one currency that has slid about 3% a year for thirty years. Owning assets that earn in dollars is how you stop that from quietly shrinking you in world terms. The details of which country are covered on the Global Finance page.

composition.name: United States
composition.note: Expensive on CAPE, but the world's best businesses and a reliable rupee tailwind

composition.name: Japan & developed Asia
composition.note: Cheaper, improving corporate governance, ageing populations

composition.name: Europe & UK
composition.note: Genuinely cheap on CAPE, slower growth, good dividends

composition.name: Other developed
composition.note: Canada, Australia — commodity-heavy

returns.label: Profit growth
returns.def: Slower than India's — these are mature economies with mature companies.

returns.label: Dividends
returns.def: Higher than India's, particularly from Europe and Japan.

returns.label: Valuation drift
returns.def: CAPE at 30 against a 22 average means expecting the price tag investors pay to drift back down. The main drag.

returns.label: Rupee weakening
returns.def: The reason this works from India. Your dollar assets are worth more rupees each year, with no effort from the companies.

assets.return_note: About 8% a year in rupees — less than Indian equity's 11-12%, which is the honest trade-off. You own this for the currency protection and the different risks, not because it will beat the Nifty.

history.label: 2000 to 2010
history.value: Roughly zero in dollars — the 'lost decade' that people forget when US shares look unbeatable

assets.worst_fall: Fell about 34% in March 2020 and 57% in 2008 in dollar terms — though the rupee's fall cushioned Indian investors both times
drivers_up: The rupee weakening, which is the base case rather than a risk
US interest rates falling
AI genuinely raising profits rather than merely raising prices
Diversification working: world shares often rise when Indian shares do not
drivers_down: A CAPE of 30, which has historically meant weak ten-year returns from the starting point
Extreme concentration — a handful of American technology companies dominate the index
Indian fund houses hitting the industry-wide overseas investment cap, which periodically halts new purchases
The rupee strengthening, which would reverse the tailwind
assets.wins_when: The rupee weakens fast, and whenever India specifically underperforms the world
assets.role: Fifteen to twenty-five per cent of equity, held permanently. Not for higher returns — for the fact that your salary, your house and your Nifty fund are all one bet on one country and one currency.

how_to_invest.examples: S&P 500, Nasdaq 100 and MSCI World feeder funds from Indian fund houses
how_to_invest.tax: 12.5% on gains after two years; at your slab if sold sooner
how_to_invest.note: Simplest route — a rupee SIP, no dollar conversion, no foreign paperwork. The catch is that SEBI's industry-wide overseas cap has repeatedly forced these schemes to stop accepting money, so check they are open.

how_to_invest.route: International ETF on an Indian exchange
how_to_invest.examples: Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 ETFs listed in India
how_to_invest.note: Cheaper, but when the overseas cap binds these can trade at a large premium to their true value. Always check the indicative value before buying.

how_to_invest.route: Direct US brokerage under the RBI scheme
how_to_invest.examples: Indian platforms offering US stock accounts, or a US broker directly
how_to_invest.cost: Conversion charges plus brokerage; 20% TDS on remittances above ₹10 lakh
how_to_invest.tax: 12.5% on gains after two years; dividends taxed in the US at 25% then credited here
how_to_invest.note: Most flexibility and most paperwork — you must declare foreign assets in your Indian tax return under Schedule FA, and failing to do so carries serious penalties.

how_to_invest.examples: Funds and platforms based in India's international financial centre
how_to_invest.note: A newer route that sits outside the mutual fund overseas cap. Growing quickly and worth watching, though the retail product range is still thin.

assets.tax: International funds are treated as non-equity in India: 12.5% on gains if held over two years, otherwise at your income slab. Direct US holdings follow the same capital gains treatment, and you must disclose them in Schedule FA of your tax return.
watch: Whether your fund is currently accepting investments — the overseas cap binds periodically
The premium on international ETFs versus their true value before you buy
The rupee-dollar rate, which is roughly a third of your return here
assets.verdict: Expensive, and still worth owning — for a reason that has nothing to do with returns. World shares at a CAPE of 30 against a long-run 22 point to about 8% a year in rupees, below Indian equity's 11-12%, so on the numbers alone you would skip this. The case is that every other thing you own is one bet: your salary, your home, your Nifty fund, your fixed deposit, all in a currency that has weakened about 3% a year for three decades. Fifteen to twenty-five per cent in dollar-earning assets is insurance against the one risk an Indian investor cannot diversify away locally. Buy it through a rupee SIP, check the fund is open, and lean toward the cheaper regions rather than piling further into the Nasdaq.

families.label: Everything else
families.note: Options that exist and that people put real money into. Included so you can judge them, not because they belong in every portfolio.

assets.name: Crypto assets
assets.metric_def: There is none. Shares have profits, bonds have interest, property has rent, gold has a 5,000-year real price history. Crypto has none of these, so there is no number that can tell you whether it is cheap or expensive — only what someone paid last.
assets.metric_avg_label: No earnings, rent or interest to compare against

extras.label: Tax on gains
extras.def: No slab benefit, no long-term rate, no deduction for costs other than the purchase price. The harshest treatment of any asset on this page.

extras.label: Losses
extras.def: A loss on one crypto asset cannot be offset against a gain on another, or against any other income, or carried forward. This is unique and it matters enormously.

extras.label: TDS on every trade
extras.def: Deducted on each sale regardless of profit. Frequent trading bleeds capital through this alone.

assets.what_it_is: Digital tokens recorded on a shared ledger. Bitcoin is the largest and is designed to be scarce; Ether underpins a network of applications. Legal to buy and hold in India, taxed severely, and not regulated as an investment product.
assets.own: A claim on nothing, whose price is entirely what the next buyer will pay. That is not a moral judgment — it is a structural description, and it is the single most important thing to understand. A share entitles you to profits, a bond to interest, a flat to rent. A token entitles you to nothing, so there is no cash flow to anchor the price and no level at which it is objectively cheap. It may still rise; it simply cannot be valued.
assets.return_note: There is deliberately no estimate here, because there is nothing to build one from. Every other asset on this page has a cash flow to anchor it — profits, interest, rent — so you can say where a return would come from even if you are wrong about the size. A token has none, so anyone quoting an expected return is guessing. What can be stated with confidence: the tax treatment is the worst of any asset available to you, and the falls are the largest.

history.label: Last 10 years
history.value: Extraordinary — and preceded by nothing that would have let you predict it

history.label: 2021 to 2022
history.value: Bitcoin fell about 77%; many smaller tokens fell 95% or went to zero

history.label: Number of failures
history.value: Several major exchanges and lenders collapsed, taking customer money with them

assets.worst_fall: Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% on four separate occasions and taken two to three years to recover each time. Smaller tokens frequently go to zero permanently
drivers_up: Institutional adoption through regulated products in the US and elsewhere
Abundant global liquidity — crypto has behaved as the most speculative end of risk appetite
Its fixed supply schedule, which is genuinely different from any government currency
Regulatory clarity, which reduces the risk of an outright ban
drivers_down: Having no valuation anchor, so there is no floor when sentiment turns
Rising real interest rates, which have hurt it more than any other asset
Exchange failures and lost keys — the loss is total and there is no deposit insurance
India's tax treatment, which makes active participation structurally unprofitable
assets.wins_when: Global liquidity is abundant and risk appetite is high; it falls hardest and fastest in any panic
assets.role: If you want exposure, treat it as money you are prepared to see go to zero — a small single-digit percentage at most, bought slowly, never with borrowed money. It has no claim on a place in a portfolio the way shares, bonds and property do.

how_to_invest.examples: Exchanges registered with India's Financial Intelligence Unit
how_to_invest.tax: 30% flat on gains, 1% TDS on each sale, no loss set-off
how_to_invest.note: FIU registration means anti-money-laundering compliance, not investor protection. There is no SEBI oversight, no compensation scheme and no regulator to complain to if the exchange fails.

how_to_invest.examples: Hardware wallets
how_to_invest.note: Removes exchange failure risk and adds total responsibility. Lose the recovery phrase and the money is gone permanently, with no recourse of any kind.

how_to_invest.examples: Spot Bitcoin ETFs listed in the US
how_to_invest.tax: Unsettled — likely 30% as a virtual digital asset; take professional advice
how_to_invest.note: Whether an Indian resident may hold these under the RBI remittance scheme is genuinely unclear. Do not assume it is permitted because a platform offers it.

how_to_invest.examples: Offshore derivative platforms
how_to_invest.tax: As above, plus possible foreign exchange law violations
how_to_invest.note: Leveraged crypto trading through offshore platforms may breach India's foreign exchange rules. This is where retail money is destroyed fastest.

assets.tax: A flat 30% on gains with no slab benefit and no long-term rate. Only the cost of acquisition may be deducted — not exchange fees or interest. Losses cannot be set off against anything, including other crypto gains, and cannot be carried forward. A 1% TDS applies to every sale. Taken together this is the most punitive tax treatment of any asset in India, and it is deliberate.
watch: Any change to the 30% rate or the loss set-off rule, which would materially change the arithmetic
Whether you would genuinely be unmoved by a 70% fall — it has happened four times
Your total position as a percentage of net worth, honestly measured
assets.verdict: The one asset here that cannot be valued, only priced — and India taxes it harder than anything else. That is not a verdict on whether it rises; it is the structural fact that matters. Every other asset on this page has something that anchors its price: profits, interest, rent, or five thousand years of real-price history. A token has none, which is why there is no number that tells you it is cheap and no floor when sentiment turns. Layer on India's rules — 30% flat, no loss set-off at all, 1% deducted on every sale — and the after-tax mathematics are worse than most holders realise. It is included here because it exists, people put real money into it, and you deserve the honest version rather than either the sales pitch or a lecture. If you want some, keep it to money you could watch go to zero without it changing your life.

gauges.name: Shares versus government bonds
gauges.metric: Nifty earnings yield minus the 10-year government bond yield
gauges.plain: Flip the PE ratio upside down and you get the "earnings yield" — the profit the companies earn for every ₹100 you pay. Right now shares earn you about 4.4% and a government bond pays about 6.6% with no risk at all. So you are accepting 2.2 points LESS to take equity risk.
gauges.meaning: That sounds mad until you remember bonds pay you the same rupee amount forever, while company profits grow. Over the last two decades the gap has averaged about −1.6 points, so today is slightly worse than normal but not extreme. When this gap gets to −4 or worse, shares have historically gone on to disappoint; when it turns positive, shares have been a gift.

gauges.name: Gold versus Indian shares
gauges.metric: Gold price divided by the Nifty 50 level
gauges.plain: One ratio, one question: how many units of the Nifty does an ounce of gold buy? When gold is high on this measure, fear has been paid for generously and shares are the cheaper of the two.
gauges.meaning: Gold has already done its job for this cycle — it rose while the world was frightened. Historically, buying gold after it has run hard against shares has produced poor 5-year returns; buying it when nobody wants it has been where the money was made. This is exactly why a fixed percentage, rebalanced, beats chasing.

gauges.name: Small companies versus large ones
gauges.metric: Nifty Smallcap 250 PE divided by Nifty 50 PE
gauges.plain: Small companies usually trade a little dearer than large ones because they can grow faster. When that premium stretches far above its normal level, you are paying up twice — for growth, and for the excitement.
gauges.meaning: Every Indian small-cap mania has ended the same way: the premium peaks, then small caps fall roughly twice as hard as the Nifty and take years longer to recover. The premium, not the price level, is the warning light.

gauges.name: Property versus lending
gauges.metric: Rental yield on a flat versus the 10-year government bond
gauges.plain: A flat rented out returns about 2.8% a year in rent before repairs, tax and empty months. Lending the same money to the Government of India pays about 6.6% with no tenant, no broker and no maintenance.
gauges.meaning: That gap means Indian property prices already have years of future rent increases built into them. Property can still win — through leverage and forced saving — but the rent alone is no longer paying you to own it.

gauges.name: Cash after inflation
gauges.metric: Bank fixed deposit rate minus tax minus inflation
gauges.plain: A 7% fixed deposit at the 30% slab leaves you 4.9%. Take away inflation of about 4.5% and you have kept roughly 0.4% of buying power.
gauges.meaning: This is the real cost of "safety": over 30 years, cash roughly preserves what you have and grows almost nothing. That is fine for money you need within three years and quietly ruinous for money you need in thirty.

regimes.name: Inflation runs hot
regimes.tell: CPI above 6%, food and fuel leading, RBI turning hawkish
winners: Gold — the classic hedge, because it cannot be printed
Commodity producers — metals and energy sell the very things getting dearer
Banks, early on — they reprice loans upward faster than deposits
losers: Long-dated bonds — a fixed 6.6% forever is worth less as prices rise
Expensive growth shares — future profits discounted harder hurt them most
Cash and FDs — the real return goes negative
regimes.why: Inflation is the tax that nobody votes for. It punishes anything promising you a FIXED number of rupees later, and rewards anything whose price rises with the general price level.
regimes.india: India's inflation is still mostly a food and fuel story. A bad monsoon or a crude spike does more to your portfolio than any Fed meeting, because it forces the RBI to keep rates high and squeezes the consumer companies that dominate the index.

regimes.name: Interest rates come down
regimes.tell: RBI cutting, bond yields falling, liquidity comfortable
winners: Long-dated bonds — the price of an existing bond rises as new ones pay less
Small and mid caps — cheaper borrowing helps smaller, more indebted firms most
Property and real-estate shares — EMIs fall, buyers return
Gold — it competes with interest-bearing assets, so lower rates help it
losers: Banks, late in the cycle — loan rates fall faster than deposit costs
Savers rolling over FDs at lower and lower rates
regimes.why: A falling interest rate raises the value of every future rupee. Assets whose payoff is far in the future — growth shares, long bonds, property — gain the most, which is why rate-cut cycles feel like everything works at once.
regimes.india: In India, rate cuts usually arrive when inflation is beaten and growth is soft. The market front-runs them by six months, so the money is made while the news still sounds bad.

regimes.name: The rupee weakens fast
regimes.tell: FII outflows, dollar index strong, RBI selling reserves
winners: IT services and pharma — they earn in dollars and spend in rupees
Gold — priced in dollars globally, so it rises in rupee terms automatically
International funds — your dollar assets are worth more rupees
losers: Oil refiners, airlines, chemical importers — their input bills are in dollars
Anyone holding only rupee assets — quietly poorer in world terms
regimes.why: A currency is a price like any other. When the rupee falls, every rupee-earning asset you own is marked down against the world, and every dollar-earning asset is marked up. Most Indian portfolios are 100% on the losing side of that trade.
regimes.india: The rupee has slid roughly 3% a year against the dollar for three decades. Treat that as the baseline weather, not an emergency — and own some dollar earnings so you are not betting everything on one currency.

regimes.name: The world gets frightened
regimes.tell: War, a banking scare, a tariff shock; VIX spiking, FIIs selling everything
winners: Gold — the one asset people buy precisely because they trust nothing else
Government bonds — money runs to whatever cannot default
Cash — optionality, the ability to buy what others must sell
losers: Small caps — the first thing sold, because they are hardest to sell later
Emerging markets broadly, India included, regardless of local news
regimes.why: In a panic, correlations go to one: things that normally move separately all fall together, because the seller is not choosing on merit — they simply need cash. Only genuinely different assets protect you, and there are very few.
regimes.india: India is fundamentally a domestic economy but a foreign-funded market. That is why a Nifty fall can have nothing to do with India: the seller is an overseas fund meeting redemptions in New York.

regimes.name: Growth is strong and boring
regimes.tell: Profits rising, inflation behaved, credit growing, no crisis in the news
winners: Shares in general, and small and mid caps most of all
Banks — loan growth with low defaults is their sweet spot
Property and cyclicals — industry, autos, construction
losers: Gold — nobody needs insurance when nothing is burning
Cash — the opportunity cost of sitting out compounds
regimes.why: This is the regime that pays owners of businesses, and it lasts longer than anyone expects. The mistake is not being absent — it is arriving late, after valuations have already priced in the good weather continuing forever.
regimes.india: India has had the longest stretches of this of any large market. It is also why Indian investors systematically underestimate how bad the other four regimes feel: most portfolios here have never been properly tested.
